title: Building Substack: Reinventing Culture through Subscriptions

reader_summary.headline: In a world of abundant content, how do I allocate my scarce attention?
reader_summary.overview: In a world of abundant content, how do I allocate my scarce attention? We're so used to the internet being this place where you can publish anything and anything can happen. I think you could make the argument that actually it's a fluke.

key_points.text: The same way that you might write a piece of software and change how a million people do their jobs.
key_points.evidence_quote: The same way that you might write a piece of software and change how a million people do their jobs, you could write a great essay and change who a million people are.

key_points.text: We're now in an era where you're not going to be able to build a billion active users at supported things.
key_points.evidence_quote: We're now in an era where you're not going to be able to build a billion active users at supported things.

key_points.text: If what I read is what I become, who do I trust for that?
key_points.evidence_quote: If what I read is what I become, who do I trust for that?

key_points.text: But today, you'll get to hear about the very origins of this company.

thesis: The episode explores the origins of Substack, detailing how its founders chose to target email technology originally developed in 1971 to address the challenge of allocating scarce attention in an era of abundant content. It also recounts the founders' prior experience building a multi-hundred million user messaging app called KICK, including their early struggles with scaling infrastructure and their evolution from coding directly to leading engineering teams.
